\chapter{Two Sibilants, One Liquid, and Three Standalone Vowels}
\label{ch:sibilant-runway}
\hlchaptermodality{8}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can write the last six signs of the second runway, and name every sign in it after four chapters' distance.}

Retrieve the whole twenty-four-sign runway at real distance, one group at a time.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la]{\mr{ल} — the plain \emph{l}, beside the curled one you know}

\label{lesson:MR-W08-la}



\begin{quote}
You learned the harder \emph{l} first. Here is the ordinary one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{ल}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{ल}} is plain \emph{la}, the tongue at the teeth — the sound English writes with \emph{l}. You already write \textbf{\mr{ळ}}, the retroflex \emph{ḷ} Marathi keeps alongside it, and which Hindi does not have at all.

Meeting the rare one first was not an accident: \textbf{\mr{ळ}} sits in \emph{kāḷjī} and \emph{ḍoḷā}, words this book needed early. Now the common one arrives, and with it \emph{bolṇe}, \textquotedblleft{}to speak\textquotedblright{}, becomes readable end to end.

\subsection*{Writing — observe and trace}
Trace \textbf{\mr{ल}} twice, then trace \textbf{\mr{ळ}} once beside it. Say \emph{la} and \emph{ḷa}, moving the tongue back only for the second.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the two does Hindi not have? (\textbf{\mr{ळ}}.)

Source: \href{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Deva-\%E0\%A4\%B2-order.gif}{Opiaterein, Devanagari la stroke animation}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[śa]{\mr{श} — the \emph{sh} at the roof of the mouth}

\label{lesson:MR-W08-sha}



\begin{quote}
You write the plain \emph{s}. Slide the tongue back along the roof of your mouth and it becomes something else.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{श}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{श}} is \emph{śa}, English \emph{sh}. Marathi keeps it distinct from the \textbf{\mr{स}} you learned in your first chapter, and the pair behaves like every other pair in this runway: same air, different place.

It opens \emph{śahar}, \textquotedblleft{}city\textquotedblright{} — one of the six labels the A1 form chapters will ask you to fill in. Draw the left hook, the upright, and the headline; the small loop at the top left is what separates it from \textbf{\mr{म}}.

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy}
Copy \textbf{\mr{श}} twice with the model visible. Then write \textbf{\mr{स}} once beside it and say both, sliding the tongue back only for the first.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which one opens \emph{śahar}? (\textbf{\mr{श}}.)

Source: \href{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Deva-\%E0\%A4\%B6-order.gif}{Opiaterein, Devanagari sha stroke animation}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ṣa]{\mr{ष} — the third sibilant, kept on the page}

\label{lesson:MR-W08-ssa}



\begin{quote}
Marathi writes three sibilants and says two. This is the third one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{ष}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{ष}} is \emph{ṣa}, the retroflex sibilant. Sanskrit distinguished it from \textbf{\mr{श}}; most Marathi speakers today say the two the same way, and keep them apart only in \textbf{spelling}.

That is worth knowing rather than hiding: a letter can survive in the writing system after the sound behind it has merged. \textbf{\mr{ष}} appears in tatsama words taken whole from Sanskrit, such as \emph{bhāṣā}, \textquotedblleft{}language\textquotedblright{} — another of the six form labels waiting for you.

\subsection*{Writing — delayed copy}
Look at \textbf{\mr{ष}} for five seconds, cover it, and write it once. Uncover and set it beside \textbf{\mr{श}}: two shapes your mouth no longer separates.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Are \textbf{\mr{श}} and \textbf{\mr{ष}} different sounds for most speakers today? (\textbf{No — different spellings.})

Source: \href{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Deva-\%E0\%A4\%B7-order.gif}{Opiaterein, Devanagari ssa stroke animation}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[u]{\mr{उ} — short \emph{u} standing on its own}

\label{lesson:MR-W08-u-independent}



\begin{quote}
You already hang a short \emph{u} under a consonant. What happens when there is no consonant to hang it on?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{उ}
\end{quote}

Then you write \textbf{\mr{उ}}, the independent short \emph{u} — the same vowel given its own full letter for the start of a word.

Devanagari does this for every vowel: a \textbf{mark} when something carries it, a \textbf{letter} when nothing does. You have already seen the pair once, with \textbf{\mr{अ}} and its mark. \textbf{\mr{उ}} opens \emph{udyā}, \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{}, in the farewell this book taught you chapters ago.

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy}
Copy \textbf{\mr{उ}} twice with the model visible. Then write the short-\emph{u} mark beside it and say aloud which of the two needs a consonant to lean on.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word for \emph{tomorrow} starts with it? (\emph{\textbf{udyā}}.)

Source: \href{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Devanagari\_\%E0\%A4\%89\_stroke\_order.svg}{Saurmandal, Devanagari u stroke order}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ū]{\mr{ऊ} — long \emph{ū} standing on its own}

\label{lesson:MR-W08-uu-independent}



\begin{quote}
One more, and this runway is finished. It is the long partner of the letter you wrote a moment ago.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{ऊ}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{ऊ}} is the independent long \emph{ū}: \textbf{\mr{उ}} with a tail carried down and to the right, the same extra travel the long mark asked for below the line.

Four forms, one vowel: \textbf{\mr{उ}} and \textbf{\mr{ऊ}} when it stands alone, the short and long marks when a consonant carries it. That symmetry is the whole vowel system of this script, and you now write all of it.

\subsection*{Writing — delayed copy}
Look at \textbf{\mr{ऊ}} for five seconds, cover it, and write it once. Uncover and set the four \emph{u} forms in a row: \textbf{\mr{उ} \mr{ऊ}} and the two marks. Repair only one.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many written forms does this one vowel have? (\textbf{Four.})

Source: \href{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Devanagari\_\%E0\%A4\%8A\_stroke\_order.svg}{Saurmandal, Devanagari uu stroke order}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[e]{\mr{ए} — the vowel that opens \emph{ek}}

\label{lesson:MR-W08-e-independent}



\begin{quote}
One vowel left, and you have been reading it since the chapter where you learned to count.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{ए}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{ए}} is the independent long \emph{e} — the same vowel as the \textbf{\mr{े}} mark you write above the headline, given its own letter for the start of a word.

It opens \textbf{\mr{एक}}, \emph{ek}, \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{}. That word has been printed beside its romanization since the counting chapter, which means you have been looking at this letter for a long time without being told what it was. Draw the left hook, the upright, and the headline; the mark version is what remains if you take the letter away and keep only the top.

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy}
Copy \textbf{\mr{एक}} twice with the model visible, naming both signs: independent \emph{e}, then \emph{ka}. Then write the \textbf{\mr{े}} mark once on its own and say which of the two forms needs a consonant to lean on.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which number word starts with \textbf{\mr{ए}}? (\emph{\textbf{ek}} — one.)

Source: \href{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Devanagari\_\%E0\%A4\%8F\_stroke\_order.svg}{Saurmandal, Devanagari e stroke order}.
\end{tcolorbox}
